data.title: Cibus Therapeutics and Greenstone Biosciences Announce First Participant Dosed in Phase 1 Trial of CBT-248 (GSB-D248), an Investigational Oral Anti-Inflammatory Therapy for Chronic Pancreatitis
data.description:
PALO ALTO, Calif. —

Cibus Therapeutics and Greenstone Biosciences today announced that the first participant has been dosed in a Phase 1 clinical trial of CBT-248 (GSB-D248), an investigational oral small-molecule therapy being developed for chronic pancreatitis and ulcerative colitis. The trial is being conducted in Australia.

CBT-248 was developed at Greenstone Biosciences and is exclusively licensed to Cibus Therapeutics, which is leading its clinical development. The compound is designed to modulate multiple inflammatory pathways, with preclinical studies demonstrating efficacy in models of chronic pancreatitis and ulcerative colitis.

Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive fibro-inflammatory disease of the pancreas that causes severe, often intractable pain, irreversible tissue damage, and loss of digestive and endocrine function. It is estimated to affect approximately 3 million people worldwide and is associated with an increased risk of pancreatic cancer. No approved disease-modifying therapy exists; current care is limited to managing symptoms and complications.

Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by persistent inflammation and ulceration of the colon, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, urgency, and fatigue. Despite advances in treatment, many patients experience inadequate responses, loss of efficacy, or intolerance to existing therapies, highlighting the continued need for safer and more effective treatments that provide sustained disease control.

The Phase 1 study is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-ascending-dose study evaluating the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of CBT-248 in healthy adult volunteers. The study plans to enroll 32 participants across four dose cohorts at Nucleus Network in Melbourne, Australia, and includes an assessment of the effect of food on drug exposure. Additional details are available on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07905053) and ANZCTR (ACTRN12626001257358). 

Data from the trial are intended to inform dose selection and the design of subsequent clinical studies in patients with chronic pancreatitis and ulcerative colitis. Cibus expects topline safety, tolerability and PK data in Q2 2027.

"Taking GSB-D248 from discovery through IND-enabling studies meant answering one question at every step: will what we see in the lab hold up in people?" said Mukhtar Ahmed, PhD, Director of Project & Portfolio Strategy at Greenstone Biosciences, who led the compound's preclinical development. "Seeing the first participant dosed is the start of getting that answer. Our team is proud to have handed Cibus a program built to make that transition, and we will keep supporting it as it moves toward patients."

“Dosing the first participant marks an important milestone in advancing CBT-248 from preclinical research into clinical development,” said Honit Piplani, PhD, Director of Translational and Clinical Science at Cibus Therapeutics. “People living with chronic pancreatitis face persistent pain, difficulty eating and uncertainty about their future, and there is no approved therapy that targets the underlying disease. This first study will establish the safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics we need to design studies in patients, and we are grateful to our partners at Greenstone Biosciences for helping us reach this point.”

"This milestone reflects the discovery and translational work our team put into CBT-248 (GSB-D248)," said Joseph Wu, MD, PhD, Co-founder of Greenstone Biosciences and a Professor of Medicine & Radiology at Stanford University. "We built the preclinical package on human-relevant models to give the program the strongest possible footing for the clinic. We delivered on the plan we set with Cibus, and we look forward to supporting the program as it advances toward patients."

data.title: BIO unveils plan for US to remain biotech’s ‘global leader’
data.description:
Two months after China unveiled a five-year plan to accelerate the ascent of its fast-rising biotechnology sector, a prominent lobbying group is pitching a policy proposal designed to help the U.S. maintain an edge in the field.

The “action plan” by the Biotechnology Innovation Organization unveiled Tuesday lays out seven priorities Congress and the Trump administration should act on to “ensure” the U.S. remains the sector’s “global leader.” Called “BioAdvance: Securing America’s Biotech Century,” it involves ways to speed up drug development, improve the nation's clinical trial infrastructure, attract investment and better support biomedical research.

BIO also calls on the U.S. to establish a “White House Office of Biotechnology” to help coordinate these plans and keep them on track. 

“This moment demands the ambition and determination that catalyzed the biotechnology revolution and made America the definitive global leader,” said BIO President and CEO John Crowley in a statement.

BIO’s proposal comes amid an escalating debate among biotech executives, investors and lawmakers as to how to respond to China’s emergence as a drugmaking force. The U.S. has long been the world’s standard-bearer in developing new medicines. Yet China has made biotech progress a strategic priority and invested heavily in the sector over the last decade or so.

That effort is now “paying off,” according to BIO. China now starts more than a quarter of the world’s clinical trials and initiates early-stage studies more quickly and cheaply. Dealmaking involving China-originated medicines has exploded of late, too. More than 100 licensing deals have been struck between Western pharmaceutical firms or biotechs and Chinese drugmakers, according to BioPharma Dive data.

China aims to make further inroads in the future. In a five-year plan released in September, the Chinese government indicated its goal is to develop at least a quarter of the world’s “first-in-class drugs” by 2030. 

So far, the U.S. has waffled between trying to slow down China’s progress or boost its own sector. The Treasury Department, for instance, has floated a proposal to add biotech to the “COINS” Act, which could limit some deals and draw greater scrutiny to U.S. biotech investments in China. That approach has yielded criticism from BIO, whose leader Crowley warned in October that the U.S. “cannot restrict our way to success.”

“We need to ensure that we do not have an overly broad approach that would create uncertainty for innovators and investors, and that may unintentionally risk weakening U.S. biotech competitiveness,” Crowley said in a statement at the time.

Prominent biotech investment firms such as RA Capital Management have voiced similar criticisms, claiming putting biotech into the COINS Act “does nothing to shore up domestic manufacturing or restrict the ability of Chinese companies to control distribution of medicines.”

Meanwhile, U.S. regulators have unveiled programs to speed up clinical testing and make the U.S. a more attractive destination for starting first-in-human studies. 

Now, BIO is trying to push the federal government to go further. Its proposal includes several ways to improve drugmaking efficiency in the U.S. while addressing structural weaknesses that slow down clinical research. Investors and CEOs interviewed by BioPharma Dive said the plan, which focuses more on shoring up America’s capabilities rather than striking back at China, is achievable and a welcome move.

“I think it’s a great list,” said Lindy Morris Fishburne, a managing partner at Breakout Ventures, which invests in early-stage life sciences startups. “But the world moves on incentives and people, and if those things are not aligned, then policy doesn’t matter.”

In its report, BIO pushed legislators and the Food and Drug Administration to adopt more flexible requirements for starting first-in-human trials, prioritize modernized alternatives to animal testing and centralize many of the processes required before testing can begin. 

“Biotechnology companies must be able to efficiently test the safety and dosage of their innovations — and iterate quickly based on those results — to attract investment for early-stage research,” the organization wrote in its proposal. 

The U.S.’ clinical trial network is currently “siloed and unevenly distributed,” creating capacity constraints for specialized Phase 1 studies and slowing down early research. As a result, many U.S.-based companies are conducting an increasing share of their early-stage drug development in countries such as China and Australia, “where the process is often faster, more predictable, and less expensive,” BIO said.

Quralis, a Cambridge, Massachusetts-based brain drug developer, launched several of its proof-of-concept trials outside of the U.S. “because the regulatory framework was not conducive” to doing so at home, said Kasper Roet, the company’s CEO.

The proposal suggests that U.S. regulators engage earlier with drug developers and clearly lay out expectations during meetings. BIO also wants policymakers to centralize approval processes across local clinical trial sites, expand the network of testing locations and create “user-friendly” tools to help doctors and patients find trials.

But those efforts — and any future plans to speed up human testing — hinge on having a fully staffed agency and leadership motivated to make those changes, according to Fishburne.

“You're going to have all this incredible technology advancing pipelines, lowering risk and answering questions earlier, and then you're going to hit this old-time bureaucratic wall,” she said.

BIO previously told the FDA in a public comment that its pilot program to accelerate early testing contains only “incremental improvements” to application reviews that are “unlikely to materially shift the timelines” for those trials or reverse the ongoing trend. Fishburne said the FDA’s efforts are welcome, but “feel more like disconnected green shoots rather than [an] overarching strategy.”

The proposal also calls on the Trump administration to put more money toward basic research through the National Institutes of Health. Last year, biotech investors and academics warned of dire long-term consequences for the life sciences if the government significantly cut NIH grant funding. Though a federal court ultimately barred a plan to cap NIH funding, many institutions are still affected by delays in grant renewals and sharp drops in dollars headed toward certain types of research, one NPR report found.

“Providing ample and predictable federal research funding” and establishing “reliable pathways” to attract talent to American universities are additional cornerstones of BIO’s proposal.

Strengthening the NIH and streamlining early clinical research are particularly important parts of BIO’s request, said Chris Bardon, a managing partner at the venture firm MPM BioImpact.

“NIH research has always been the name of the game,” Bardon said. “To really undermine that is, at the end of the day, what's going to harm the long-term competitiveness of our basic science as well as of our biotechnology industry.”

BIO pointed to other legislative initiatives to spur venture capital funding and protect intellectual property rights. Policymakers “should also reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens and adopt tax and economic incentives that encourage investment in innovative startups,” the organization wrote.

A new White House Office of Biotechnology could help carry these initiatives out and ensure the government adopts a “unified national strategy.” That office could also help identify "key policy priorities to promote U.S. biotech competitiveness" and coordinate plans with "trusted allies.” 

Bardon said the BioAdvance plan could turn into a “bipartisan effort” to shore up an industry that has been “taken for granted.”

“The rise of China has woken up the United States to realize we were very comfortable being in the leading position, but now that is being challenged,” said Roet, Quralis’ CEO.

data.title: Biotech startups are built on venture capital. Track funding rounds here.
data.description:
Drug development is an expensive, risky endeavor. Biotechnology companies just starting out are many years away from seeing profits, if ever. So more often than not, a startup’s success turning science into medicines can come down to how much money it raises. That’s where venture capitalists step in, investing many millions of dollars for stakes in newly formed companies.

Young drugmakers rely on these private partners to survive until they can reach major milestones like entering clinical testing, or going public. And over the past two decades, they’ve had more and more help. The amount of money put into biotech has climbed considerably, resulting in the creation of hundreds of new companies.

Tracking that investment can reveal important patterns, showing how different drug types or diseases rise or fall out of favor with investors. BioPharma Dive built this database to help make that larger picture clear.

We’ve focused on a group of 26 venture capital firms that are highly active in creating new drug developers. In the database below, we’ve collected funding rounds involving those firms, a ledger of investment that we’ll update regularly.

If we’ve missed anything, or there’s additional information you’d like to see, please reach out and let us know.

Clicking any underlined term in the main database at right will filter by that term. Click the down arrow at far right to expand the information displayed for each round.

If the data do not display below, please try clearing your browser’s cache and reloading the page. If you still have issues, email BioPharma Dive editors for further troubleshooting.

Loading...

Methodology and limitations:

For this database, BioPharma Dive compiled venture fundraising rounds for private biotechnology companies developing human medicines. We screened for rounds involving at least one of a group of 26 highly active venture capital firms involved in company creation.

This group was selected by comparing data from SVB, HSBC, William Blair and Bay Bridge Bio that identified the most active biotech venture capital firms in 2023 and 2024 (SVB, HSBC, William Blair), 2022 (SVB), 2021 (SVB) and in 2018 to 2023 (Bay Bridge Bio). Investment activity in those lists was defined by the number of fundraising rounds in which each firm participated that year.

We then eliminated firms that were primarily a “crossover” investor. That yielded a list of 26 venture capital firms.

This core group of 26 firms is narrow by definition. But the activity of these firms provides a meaningful snapshot of investment trends in the industry. Over time, we plan to expand on this initial database by adding in more firms that meet our target focus.

This database is similarly limited by time. We focused on rounds that were completed and announced on or after Jan. 1, 2022. This captures a period of time in which the biotech sector experienced a downturn after a record high and the sector’s subsequent recovery. We also plan to add historical data from prior to Jan. 1, 2022 in later updates.

For each round identified, we collected information on the relevant company’s drugmaking modality and therapeutic area of focus, as well as the company’s stage of development and lead investors, if not one of the core group of 26 firms.

We generally used a company’s lead program to determine its modality, therapeutic area of focus and stage of development at the time of each round’s completion. The only exceptions to this are companies that inherited a late-stage candidate, but identified an earlier candidate as their priority and reason for raising funds. We categorized companies’ phase of development by the latest stage begun at the time of financing. So a company raising money to start a Phase 2 clinical trial that it hadn’t yet begun would be classified as in Phase 1.

The modalities listed are broadly defined and may not precisely describe an individual company’s experimental drug(s). They were chosen to better show overall trends in investment activity. “Drug discovery,” as a category, is meant to indicate those companies exploring new areas of science broadly, rather than focusing on a specific type of medicine.

Similarly, therapeutic areas cover a large number of diseases and, in some cases, such as with rare conditions, overlap with others. Common diseases that didn’t fit in the categories listed, such as those primarily affecting the heart, lungs, kidneys and endocrine system, were classified under “other.” When companies identified more than one therapeutic area with equal priority, we classified them as working on “multiple” therapeutic areas. Those that identified multiple areas, but prioritized one over others were classified under that priority area.

The nomenclature of venture capital rounds is fairly consistent, but some firms did not identify whether their round was seed or Series A, B, C, etc. In those cases, we classified the round as “undisclosed.” Extensions, expansions, or other add-on raises to an earlier Series round are noted, but not classified separately.

Nearly all rounds were announced in U.S. dollars. A handful were priced in euros or other foreign currencies, which we converted to dollars using exchange rate data from the relevant country’s central bank on the day the round was announced.

We organized rounds by the date they were announced, which in some cases is much later than when the round was actually raised if a company was initially operating in stealth. We did this for consistency, and to better match when a round’s existence was public knowledge. 

BioPharma Dive will update this database as rounds that meet our screening criteria are announced, but there may be some delay in when new rounds are added.

data.title: Woven Wins Healthcare Marketing Impact Award Gold for HCP VR Experience Created for BridgeBio
data.description:
NEW YORK —

Woven Health Collective has won a 2026 Healthcare Marketing Impact Award Gold for “From Clues to Clarity: Recognizing ATTR-CM,” a virtual reality experience created for BridgeBio. Presented by Modern Healthcare and Ad Age, the Technology-Driven Campaign of the Year award recognizes strategic, creative, and results-driven health care marketing and communications.

The program brings together scientific understanding, creative storytelling, and immersive technology to help health care professionals explore the experience of a patient living with undiagnosed transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, or ATTR-CM. Through a patient’s perspective, the experience connects symptoms that can be difficult to recognize when considered separately.

“Effective health care communication requires more than presenting information. It requires finding a way to make that information meaningful to the people who need it,” said Jeanne Martel, CEO and Founder of Woven Health Collective. “This recognition celebrates what becomes possible when science, creativity, and technology work together around a clear educational purpose.”

Developed in four months, the experience combines motion-capture animation, visual and audio cues, and subtle haptic feedback to bring the patient’s perspective to life. It was introduced internally to BridgeBio’s field force before reaching HCP audiences at the Heart Failure Society of America and American Heart Association Annual Scientific Meeting 2026. The program generated approximately 100 unique, in-depth engagements across key conferences.

“We wanted clinicians to encounter familiar symptoms from an unfamiliar perspective,” said Dennis Leahy, Chief Creative Officer of Woven Health Collective. “The creative idea was to bring individual symptoms together through the patient’s story. Virtual reality gave us a way to make those connections tangible, with every creative choice designed to help clinicians see the larger clinical picture.”

The award recognizes a program designed to make complex disease education more engaging and to encourage health care professionals to consider how individual symptoms may form a larger clinical picture.

Learn more about Woven’s creative and technological capabilities at: https://www.wovenhc.com.

data.title: Biotech IPOs are the industry’s lifeblood. Track how they’re performing.
data.description:
Initial public offerings make the biotechnology industry tick. Stock listings give young companies the funding they need to develop their drugs, and their venture backers an opportunity to earn a return.

For much of the past decade, biotechs found Wall Street receptive to their pitches. Public investment, drawn in by scientific advances and company successes, bolstered generations of new drugmakers.

IPO activity reached a peak in 2021, when more than 100 biotechs priced an initial offering and together raised nearly $15 billion. But that momentum came to a halt in 2022 as stock prices of newly public companies plummeted amid a sector-wide downturn. The pace of IPOs stalled and, last year, only 11 drugmakers priced initial share sales.

Emerging biotechs now face a tougher road to public markets. Which will make it? Which create value and which fail? What types of companies earn the best returns? Who are their investors?

Biopharma Dive is tracking these questions in the database below, which will be updated regularly. If we've missed anything, or there's any additional information you'd like to see, please reach out and let us know.

data.title: Making the ‘impossible’ executable in life sciences construction
data.description:
Some of the most consequential conversations we have with life sciences clients start with a request that does not have an obvious answer. It might mean adapting an existing structure that was never intended to support a life sciences facility, incorporating a material that would not typically be considered for this environment, fitting process equipment into a building that was never designed for it or completing critical work around operations that cannot stop.

The scale of the project does not always reflect its complexity. A tightly contained renovation inside an operating facility can carry more execution risk than a much larger new build. The challenge may involve an active utility system or a fixed shutdown window. In other cases, it requires the team to rethink something much more fundamental about the way the facility will be built.

Any of these situations may impact a project’s goal if solutions are not developed early. For a manufacturer, this could mean a missed production window or capacity that is unavailable when the business needs it. In a research environment, it can disrupt studies that depend on continuity.

For life sciences owners, these challenges demand a technical builder with the field experience and technical depth to work through constraints the team may not have seen before.

When ‘impossible’ is really an unresolved constraint

At DPR Construction, we recently saw this with a long-time client pursuing an ambitious sustainability goal that called for using wood in and around a manufacturing environment, a material not typically considered for this type of facility.

The team’s first reaction was hesitation. How will we incorporate material into an environment where we have been trained for years to treat it a certain way. We had to think about cleanability, operations and long-term performance to make it work.

That was the point. The client trusted us with an idea that challenged convention. It took technical depth, curiosity and a willingness to question what had always been done. Our job was to understand the risks and find a way to make it work in operation.

The same thinking applies to less unusual challenges. Equipment, utilities, structure, quality requirements and field conditions are all connected. On a complex project, different people may have insight into different aspects of the solution. The builder has to understand those connections well enough to help the team focus on what is actually driving execution.

Getting the right people involved early

There is a lot riding on these decisions. EY reported in its 2026 Biotech Beyond Borders report that industry leaders have pledged upward of $370 billion toward U.S. manufacturing as companies respond to changing trade conditions and look for more resilient supply strategies.

On a biomanufacturing project, something as basic as confirming a vendor’s equipment dimensions and utility requirements can affect structural loading, MEP routing and even how the equipment will get into the building. If that information arrives late, the team may be forced to solve in the field what could have been more efficiently and effectively handled during planning.

Integrated delivery methods help keep those conversations connected. Designers, trade partners, equipment vendors, facilities teams and builders can work through the implications as the design develops rather than handing information from one group to the next as the project unfolds.

Field knowledge also needs to be part of that process. With self-perform capability, here is a direct connection to how work will be staffed and installed. Labor assumptions can be tested against what teams are seeing in the market. Constructability questions can be discussed with people who understand the installation. If the original approach needs to change, there is more information available to make that decision.

The value is in getting these types of questions and possible solutions into the conversation early enough to shape the plan from the outset.

Why life sciences demands a different standard

Life sciences facilities carry a layer of risk that most other building types don’t: the construction itself can compromise the product. Airflow, pressure relationships and surface materials aren’t just performance considerations, they’re contamination control points, and construction activity has the ability to affect all three.

That’s part of what made the wood decision mentioned earlier so complicated. Wood is porous, it interacts with humidity, and in most manufacturing contexts it raises immediate questions about cleanability and microbial risk, questions that don’t come up the same way with steel or concrete. Solving for that required more than a structural engineer; it required people who understood how a material behaves under the same quality and regulatory scrutiny as the product being manufactured.

In an operating cGMP environment, the construction team also needs to understand the facility’s quality requirements as well as its physical ones. Planning may include clean-build protocols, contamination controls, temporary utilities, equipment interfaces and shutdowns, each one connected to a validated process that can’t be compromised without consequences far beyond the construction schedule. Facilities, quality and operations teams often need to be part of these decisions because they know what can be interrupted and what must remain protected.

A shutdown that looks manageable on a schedule can be much more complicated once you understand the systems it touches. A utility tie-in can have implications well beyond the room where the work takes place.

This is where life sciences experience matters most: understanding that every material and sequencing decision carries regulatory weight, not just a schedule or budget one.

The work also needs to support what comes next. Construction helps position the facility for commissioning, qualification and validation, while the owner retains responsibility for its process, quality systems and regulatory obligations. A good construction plan considers this handoff from the beginning.

Building for the next challenge

Turnover is only one point in the life of a facility. Equipment will change. Processes will evolve. A client may come back with a small renovation that carries just as much operational risk as the original capital project.

Over time, the project team builds knowledge and experience that is difficult to recreate from drawings alone. They understand how this and other similar sites operate, where the sensitive systems are and how life sciences customers make decisions.

This is the kind of relationship DPR Construction builds with clients over time. When the next constraint or outside the box idea comes up, there is already enough trust to put the hard idea on the table and work through it together.

The next challenge may look completely different from the last one. It may even sound impossible at first. With the right people, the right technical experience and a clear understanding of how the facility actually operates, the real problem-solving can begin.

data.title: Ramaswamy’s biotech baggage haunted his political run
data.description:
Vivek Ramaswamy lost Ohio’s governor’s race Tuesday amid a surge of Democratic support. It ended pretty ugly.

In the final days before the midterm elections, six biotech leaders publicly urged him to withdraw a television ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent, Amy Acton, arguing that it ignored documented childhood trauma and betrayed the evidence-based standards of their industry. The ad had already drawn criticism from both parties. Ramaswamy, who was running as a Republican, defended it.

It was an unusually pointed rebuke from within the industry that had helped make Ramaswamy famous.

It also raises a question that tends to get skipped when he’s characterized as a ”successful biotech entrepreneur”: Successful at what?

The description isn’t invented. Roivant, the company he founded, built a network of specialized drug developers known as “Vants.” Axovant Sciences was its Alzheimer’s-focused subsidiary; other Vants went on to develop approved medicines and complete major deals. A 2023 PharmaVoice profile recalled how he had been hailed as a biotech wunderkind.

But there’s a difference between raising money and creating shareholder value with producing clinical evidence that holds up. Those distinctions matter when a business record becomes a political credential.

I helped tell an earlier version of that story. In September 2017, I brought Ramaswamy and four Roivant executives together for a Fortune interview and photo shoot. At the time, Roivant had just secured $1.1 billion in financing led by SoftBank, none of its Vants had an approved medicine and Axovant was awaiting pivotal Alzheimer’s trial results.

I called the turnkey business model audacious. I reported the risks. Still, the gravitational pull was obvious: The people had heavyweight pedigrees, the money was spectacular and the founder had a hell of a pitch.

What they didn’t yet have was proof that the lead drug worked.

The money was real, but the evidence was mixed

Not everyone waited for hindsight to ask harder questions. In June 2015, before Axovant’s IPO, reporter Adam Feuerstein examined the hedge-fund relationships and unusual financing terms behind the Alzheimer’s company.

His reporting examined the valuation investors were placing on an unproven drug and the financial terms offered to certain participants in the IPO.

The underlying bargain was stark. In December 2014, Roivant’s Axovant acquired intepirdine from GlaxoSmithKline for $5 million upfront, plus potential later payments.

By then, GSK had already completed two large phase 2 studies involving 576 and 684 patients, respectively. Conducted between 2008 and 2010, neither met its overall efficacy goals; the results were published in May 2015, after Axovant acquired the drug.

But some findings in patients also taking donepezil, an existing Alzheimer’s treatment, looked encouraging, justifying more research in that direction. The overall clinical evidence still did not establish that intepirdine worked.

Axovant nevertheless sold 24.15 million shares at $15 apiece in 2015, raising $362.3 million gross and $334.5 million net for the company. The SEC IPO prospectus also disclosed that Ramaswamy’s mother and brother, both employees, had been granted options covering 262,500 and 750,000 shares, respectively, at a 90-cent exercise price.

Two hedge funds, RA Capital and Visium Asset Management, bought a combined $150 million of Axovant shares at the $15 IPO price. They agreed not to sell for 90 days, while existing shareholders and executives generally faced 180-day restrictions. Other public IPO buyers could trade immediately.

What mattered was the timing: The funds became eligible to sell in September 2015, before Axovant began enrolling patients in its pivotal phase 3 trial that October.

Separately, the options granted to Ramaswamy’s mother and brother carried 90-cent exercise prices and four-year vesting schedules, creating potential gains tied to the share price.

The financing offered opportunities to benefit from Axovant’s valuation before the pivotal efficacy results arrived in 2017. The filings do not establish that anyone exercised options, sold shares or realized profits.

Ramaswamy’s public presentation was less qualified than the data. In an October 2015 CNBC interview, he said intepirdine was “statistically significantly better than the placebo.”

By the time Ramaswamy made those comments, Axovant had acquired the drug, completed its IPO and had access to the earlier GSK evidence. Its pivotal phase 3 trial testing intepirdine in combination with donepezil would begin enrolling patients later that month.

A preliminary analysis co-authored by his mother, an Axovant employee, had emphasized favorable results for the combination. But as PolitiFact recently documented, his comments did not clearly distinguish positive findings for intepirdine in combination with donepezil from the broader, disappointing trial record.

And then on Sept. 26, 2017, Axovant announced that its 1,315-patient phase 3 Mindset trial had missed both primary endpoints. No statistically significant improvement in cognition. None in daily functioning.

The stock collapsed. The clinic had delivered a much less marketable answer than the financing rounds.

During the Ohio gubernatorial race, Acton’s campaign claimed Ramaswamy made “hundreds of millions of dollars” pushing an Alzheimer’s drug “he knew didn’t work.” PolitiFact rated that assertion “Mostly False.” There was a gap between what the available studies established and what an investor or patient might have understood from the pitch.

The problem was not that he pursued a risky drug, and Axovant’s willingness to take on a late-stage study for intepirdine indicated some level of scientific conviction in its potential, PolitiFact pointed out. Axovant’s IPO proceeds were also corporate funds, not his personal take-home pay.

Ultimately, the trial failure did not establish advance knowledge or fraud.

Ramaswamy’s long shadow

He left Roivant’s day-to-day CEO role in 2021 and resigned from its board in 2023. By then, Roivant said six medicines developed at companies it launched had won FDA approval.

Under successor CEO Matt Gline, Roivant sold its 75% stake in Telavant, a joint venture with Pfizer, as part of Roche’s approximately $7.1 billion acquisition completed in December 2023.

PharmaVoice chronicled that deal and later interviewed Gline about pursuing overlooked opportunities in drug development. It is a record of real business achievement, not a company that disappeared with Axovant.

Roivant’s leadership also publicly distinguished its work from its founder’s political rhetoric.

During his brief bid to become the Republican presidential nominee in 2023, Ramaswamy invoked his biotech credentials to accuse the FDA of corruption and propose gutting the agency. STAT’s Feuerstein and Matthew Herper examined his claims and found serious factual problems. Gline publicly disagreed with the FDA attack.

“I think he’s wrong about the FDA,” Gline told The Wall Street Journal in a 2023 interview republished by Mint. “We have a lot of respect for them as our regulator.”

In a later PharmaVoice interview, Gline described the need to be “ruthlessly data-driven.” That’s a striking contrast in emphasis, though it does not erase what Ramaswamy contributed to building Roivant.

A Roivant spokesperson said the company had no comment on questions for this article. Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to a separate request for comment.

What’s the takeaway from Ramaswamy’s journey from biotech to politics?

Executive firepower, huge checks and founder mythology can set a certain tempo, but the actual clinical proposition isn't as forgiving.

Ramaswamy told Fortune a decade ago that Roivant’s “ultimate measure of success” would be whether it could validate its clinical bets and bring them to patients.

That same month, Axovant’s ostensibly star candidate missed both its primary clinical endpoints. And now Ramaswamy has lost two high-profile attempts to make it big in politics.

Wherever he goes next, “successful biotech entrepreneur” might remain a permanent line in his biography. These facts are a part of that story too.

data.title: This week in charts: 3 drug launches Wall Street is watching
data.description:
This is the latest installment in a series where BioPharma Dive uses data visualization to recap what’s going on across the industry. Today, we’re looking at how investors reacted to three drug launches featured in quarterly earnings presentations this week. 

Novo has struggled mightily to regain its footing after ceding its leadership position in obesity drugs to top rival Eli Lilly. But a key sales figure the Danish drugmaker disclosed this week provided investors with some optimism that better times are ahead.

On Wednesday, Novo revealed that the Wegovy pill — the oral version of the popular obesity medicine bearing the same name — booked 5.39 billion Danish kroner in the third quarter. Equivalent to about $811 million, that figure surpassed the average consensus estimate of 4.96 billion kroner, according to analysts at the firm Jefferies. Overall company sales and profit beat Wall Street’s projections, too. 

The news lifted Novo shares by more than 5%, one of its largest single-day gains this year. Perhaps more notably, though, the Wegovy pill’s sales spike came during the same quarter Lilly’s rival offering, Foundayo, underperformed. Lilly’s drug launched a few months after Novo’s, and isn’t as broadly available yet. But its $184 million in third-quarter sales fell short of Wall Street estimates by $44 million and represented the only blemish for an obesity and diabetes drug franchise that otherwise smashed consensus forecasts. 

The Wegovy pill “continued to outpace” Foundayo and accounted for around 80% of new-to-brand U.S. prescriptions in the third quarter, said Jamey Millar, the head of Novo’s U.S. operations, on a Wednesday earnings call.

Novo is counting on an upswing in the U.S. and internationally to continue. “I don't foresee why that should completely change,” CEO Mike Doustdar told analysts. “How well we’ve done both in the U.S. and [internationally] does not change just because January comes after December.”

The pill has launched in seven countries so far. Novo expects it to be available in more than 20 by early next year.

Sales of Novo's Wegovy pill took off in the third quarter

Drug sales surpassed Wall Street expectations after falling short of forecasts in the previous earnings period.

Madrigal Pharmaceuticals made history with the 2024 approval of Rezdiffra, the first medication for a liver disease known as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, or “MASH.” Since then, Wall Street has been closely tracking Rezdiffra’s progress, as the drug’s sales trajectory is an important indicator of the demand for MASH drugs. Many investors weren’t convinced Rezdiffra would become a big seller.     

New results disclosed this week, though, show that Rezdiffra sales — which got off to a better-than-anticipated start — are still climbing. In its tenth quarter on the market, the drug officially reached “blockbuster” status, meaning its sales eclipsed $1 billion in a calendar year. Rezdiffra generated $431 million for Madrigal between July and September, and $1.1 billion so far in 2026. The quarterly numbers beat consensus projections by more than $20 million and enabled Madrigal to post a profit for the first time. 

The results “couldn’t have been better” and “exceeded even elevated investor expectations,” wrote Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Prakhar Agrawal in a Tuesday client note. 

Particularly of note, according to Agrawal, is that more patients have started treatment despite competition in MASH from Novo’s Wegovy. That upswing suggests MASH diagnosis and treatment rates — both of which are still low — could be accelerating. There’s “meaningful room for growth,” he added. 

Madrigal shares initially spiked before changing course on Tuesday, a shift analysts attributed to a whistleblower lawsuit brought forth by a former employee.

Madrigal's MASH drug Rezdiffra has become a blockbuster

Rezdiffra generated $1.1 billion in sales over the first nine months of 2026.

Five months ago, brain drug developer Axsome Therapeutics saw its market value soar past $12 billion. An April Food and Drug Administration approval had just expanded use of its depression drug Auvelity into Alzheimer’s disease, unlocking what Wall Street believed to be a multibillion-dollar market opportunity. Investors piled into the stock, believing Axsome might be a top buyout target in an already active year for biotech company acquisitions. 

Yet at least so far, Auvelity hasn’t taken off. Sales grew from about $153 million between January and March to $208 million over the last three months, Axsome reported Monday. On a conference call with analysts, Chief Commercial Officer Ari Maizel noted that there’s “little precedent” for a medicine that, like Auvelity, is used to treat symptoms of “agitation” associated with Alzheimer’s.

“This is still a relatively new and developing market, but we're very encouraged by what we've seen thus far,” Maizel said, citing upticks in prescription totals. 

Auvelity sales haven't climbed as quickly as investors had hoped

Quarterly sales, in millions, of Auvelity, which was approved for Alzheimer's disease agitation in April.

Investors appear less sure. Since peaking in June, Axsome’s stock price has fallen by more than a third. The pace of drugmaker acquisitions has slowed. And though Auvelity’s latest figures were in line with consensus estimates, the drug’s latest launch is off to a “slower than expected” start, wrote William Blair analyst Myles Minter. A few of his peers at other firms went a step further, trimming their price targets for Axsome shares and projections for Auvelity sales. 

“It’s been a very difficult four months” for Axsome, wrote Leerink Partners analyst Marc Goodman. Investors now “seem to have significant pessimism regarding Auvelity trends.”

Still, he and others preached patience. During the third quarter, prescription totals accelerated in adults over 65, who are mostly using Auvelity for Alzheimer’s symptoms, executives said. While the drug’s sales upswing has been gradual, “it’s happening,” Goodman asserted.

data.title: Numbers Show More Biotech Sponsors Turn to Kivo to Keep TMFs and Assets Diligence-Ready
data.description:
PORTLAND, Ore. —

Kivo, the GxP-compliant document and process management platform for life sciences teams, today announced over 200 percent growth in biotech sponsors keeping their trial master files (TMFs) and regulatory assets on its platform, as more clinical-stage companies adopt its GxP-compliant solution to increase attractiveness to investors and acquirers. Sponsors now manage more than 3,000 drug programs in Kivo.

Kivo supports drug programs throughout their journey, from preclinical development through Phase 1, Phase 2, and Phase 3 clinical trials and ultimately toward regulatory approval, partnership, or acquisition. By bringing Regulatory, Clinical, and Quality operations together, Kivo helps ensure that the data and documents surrounding an asset are always ready for audits, inspections, and due diligence.

“Having more than 3,000 drug programs managed in Kivo represents a real shift in the industry,” said Toban Zolman, CEO of Kivo. “Guiding drugs through testing and approval is hard enough. The systems behind it shouldn’t make it harder. Our job is to remove the friction from GxP compliance so teams can focus on advancing great science and getting it closer to patients.”

Kivo Customers Landed $3 Billion in Investment in the Last Year 

In today's investment climate, maintaining diligence-ready documents creates a distinct advantage. Early-stage biotechs are increasingly choosing to manage their assets in a validated, GxP-compliant system from the start, rather than trying to store and share their pre-clinical documents and data rooms from a file-sharing system.

In the last year alone, customers of Kivo attracted more than $3 billion in investment capital, citing this as one of their reasons for growth. 

This reinforces the importance of keeping a drug program ready throughout its lifecycle, as investment rounds, partnership discussions, due diligence, and acquisition opportunities arise. Having the underlying documents, data, and regulated processes organized and ready helps teams move more quickly in these circumstances.

More Sponsors are Using Kivo to Take Ownership of the TMF

More sponsors are also bringing their TMFs into Kivo, either to manage active trials directly or to take custody of the TMF from their CRO at study close. In addition to the need for inspection readiness, the shift also reflects the impact of the ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice guideline, adopted by the FDA last year, which reinforces that sponsors remain responsible for, and should maintain control of, their essential trial records and data. 

As a member of the CDISC Vendor Committee, Kivo has also participated in the development of the new TMF Reference Model standard. Kivo will host a webinar on the TMF Reference Model on Thursday, November 12. Register here to attend: Unpacking TMF Standard Model V1.

See what's behind the momentum with a self-guided tour of the Kivo platform.

data.title: Biotech M&A is accelerating. Track the deals that are happening here.
data.description:
In the business of drug development, deals can be just as important as scientific breakthroughs. Many of today's most lucrative medicines, from the life-saving cancer treatment Keytruda to the anti-inflammatory agent Enbrel, might not have become so without mergers and acquisitions.

The end of the last decade brought record highs in pharmaceutical M&A as larger companies turned again and again to young biotechs for innovation. Often, these deals focused on cancer, rare diseases and immune system disorders — areas of drug research that were seeing major victories in clinical trials and huge profits for treatments that made it to market.

2021 and 2022 were much quieter for dealmaking, as new challenges and then rising interest rates weighed on negotiations. But there have been signs of a rebound. Pharma companies are keen to expand in areas like obesity, while stocking up on newer technologies like antibody-drug conjugates. Even neuroscience, which large drugmakers previously abandoned, is drawing investment again.

BioPharma Dive is tracking M&A activity below. The database, which shows drugmaker buyouts that have happened since 2018 and were valued at $50 million or more in upfront consideration, will be regularly updated.

Click on an acquiring company to pull up more information, and scroll to the bottom of the page to read how this information was collected and organized. If there's anything we've missed, or any additional information you'd like to see, please reach out and let us know.
